claims.text: Wear resistance of HEA protective coatings is primarily governed by formation of a protective tribo-oxidation layer during wear.
Higher concentrations of an oxide-forming element such as Ti accelerate protective tribo-oxidation-layer formation.
The proposed baseline is an as-deposited HEA coating containing a nominal concentration of the oxide-forming element.
The controlled intervention is to vary the oxide-forming-element concentration while keeping the other alloying elements and processing parameters constant.
The relevant structural mediator is an in situ protective tribo-oxidation layer, potentially containing a spinel phase, on the wear surface.
Increasing the oxide-forming-element concentration enhances the kinetics of tribo-oxidation during wear.
Increasing the oxide-forming-element concentration increases the extent of tribo-oxidation during wear.
Enhanced tribo-oxidation produces a thicker and more robust protective layer.
A thicker and more robust tribo-oxidation layer reduces material loss.
Coatings with increased oxide-forming-element content will form a more prominent tribolayer than the baseline.
Coatings with increased oxide-forming-element content will have lower wear rates than the baseline.
Coatings with reduced oxide-forming-element content will show diminished tribolayer formation.
Coatings with reduced oxide-forming-element content will have higher wear rates than the baseline.
The proposed mechanism should operate when oxidation is thermodynamically favored, particularly at higher temperatures and loads.
The proposed mechanism may not operate at low temperature or in inert atmospheres because those conditions limit oxidation.
The quantitative relationship among oxide-forming-element concentration, tribolayer thickness, and wear rate may depend on the alloy system and test conditions.
